Jointly Optimizing Debiased CTR and Uplift for Coupons Marketing: A Unified Causal Framework

Abstract.

In online advertising, marketing interventions such as coupons introduce significant confounding bias into Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction. Observed clicks reflect a mixture of users’ intrinsic preferences and the uplift induced by these interventions. This causes conventional models to miscalibrate base CTRs, which distorts downstream ranking and billing decisions. Furthermore, marketing interventions often operate as multi-valued treatments with varying magnitudes, introducing additional complexity to CTR prediction.

To address these issues, we propose the Unified Multi-Valued Treatment Network (UniMVT). Specifically, UniMVT disentangles confounding factors from treatment-sensitive representations, enabling a full-space counterfactual inference module to jointly reconstruct the debiased base CTR and intensity-response curves. To handle the complexity of multi-valued treatments, UniMVT employs an auxiliary intensity estimation task to capture treatment propensities and devise a unit uplift objective that normalizes the intervention effect. This ensures comparable estimation across the continuous coupon-value spectrum. UniMVT simultaneously achieves debiased CTR prediction for accurate system calibration and precise uplift estimation for incentive allocation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and industrial datasets demonstrate UniMVT’s superiority in both predictive accuracy and calibration. Furthermore, real-world A/B tests confirm that UniMVT significantly improves business metrics through more effective coupon distribution.

Keywords: 
Multi-valued Treatment, Debiased CTR Prediction, Causal Inference

1. Introduction

Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction (Ma et al., 2018a; Yang et al., 2021; Mao et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2023a; Fu et al., 2025) remains a cornerstone of modern recommendation and advertising systems. Its evolution has been significantly driven by Multi-Task Learning (MTL) (Caruana, 1997; Li et al., 2023a; Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2019; Bi et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Su et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2024) architectures, such as MMoE (Ma et al., 2018b) and PLE (Tang et al., 2020), which exploit correlations across diverse user behaviors to improve overall performance. However, modern industrial systems increasingly deploy proactive marketing interventions, such as discount coupons and personalized incentives, to further stimulate user engagement. As illustrated in Figure 1(a), the presence of coupons significantly shifts the observed click probability for identical user-item pairs compared to the untreated scenario. In these cases, the observed click signal is a mixture of users’ intrinsic preferences and the uplift induced by these interventions. This entanglement is further complicated by the inherent heterogeneity in user responses: high-propensity users may convert based on interest alone, making incentives redundant, while price-sensitive users often require substantial discounts. Although stronger incentives generally boost conversion, they also incur higher costs. Accurately capturing these heterogeneous treatment effects is therefore essential for moving beyond traditional CTR prediction toward a more nuanced, incentive-aware recommendation paradigm.

Uplift modeling provides the theoretical foundation for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects. Specifically, S-Learner and T-Learner (Künzel et al., 2019) serve as foundational meta-learning frameworks that utilize standard supervised models to isolate variations across different treatment groups. To mitigate selection bias in observational data, CFRNet (Shalit et al., 2017) introduces representation balancing to minimize the distribution discrepancy between treated and control populations in a latent space, while FlexTENet (Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021) adaptively shares information across potential outcomes to exploit structural similarities through flexible inductive biases. To handle continuous or multi-valued treatment intensities, DRNet (Schwab et al., 2020) partitions the intensity space into discrete intervals for localized estimation, whereas VCNet (Nie et al., 2021) leverages varying coefficient networks to ensure the functional continuity of estimated intensity-response curves. Additionally, CEVAE approximates latent factors that confound treatment assignments through variational autoencoders, and more recently, DESCN (Zhong et al., 2022) employs cross-networks to perform estimation across the entire sample space to alleviate data sparsity.

Despite these advancements, applying existing frameworks to continuous industrial interventions reveals two critical limitations: 1) Architectural isolation and data fragmentation: As shown in Figure 1(b)(i), conventional approaches often deploy uplift modeling as an isolated downstream module trained exclusively on treated samples. Consequently, the upstream CTR model remains blind to interventions, yielding biased predictions that undermine downstream calibration. Furthermore, restricting uplift training to this narrow sub-population exacerbates data sparsity and hinders the learning of robust user representations. 2) Confounding bias and calibration drift: As illustrated in Figure 1(b)(ii), even when CTR and uplift predictions are integrated into a unified model, historical treatment assignments remain heavily confounded by user features due to selection bias. Failing to explicitly disentangle intrinsic user preferences from treatment-sensitive responses across the entire sample space induces calibration drift, yielding unreliable baseline CTR and uplift predictions.

To overcome these dual bottlenecks, it is imperative to integrate CTR debiasing and continuous uplift estimation into a unified, entire-space framework. To address these challenges, we propose a unified causal modeling paradigm named UniMVT (Unified Multi-Valued Treatment Network). At the architectural level, UniMVT employs a Deconfounded Causal Representation (DCR) layer to disentangle invariant confounding variables from treatment-sensitive features. Methodologically, we decouple the estimation of base CTR and incremental uplift by introducing a Counterfactual X-Network. Crucially, we propose a Latent Unit Sensitivity (uCATE) formulation. By enforcing a latent monotonic linear treatment shift strictly within the logit space, UniMVT intrinsically captures the non-linear saturation effect of continuous intervention, providing robust and granular criteria for optimal ROI-constrained coupon allocation.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    Unified Inference Paradigm: We develop a treatment-aware CTR inference framework incorporating monotonic constraints to capture the heterogeneity of user sensitivities across varying treatment intensities, enabling simultaneous global CTR debiasing and precise uplift estimation.

  • •

    Causal Framework: We develop a causal full-space framework featuring a Deconfounded Causal Representation (DCR) layer to isolate confounding factors, and a Counterfactual X-Network that mutually regularizes factual and counterfactual predictions to bridge the observational gap.Theoretical analysis demonstrates the framework’s convergence.

  • •

    Industrial Deployment: Extensive experiments on both robust synthetic benchmarks and a massive real-world dataset demonstrate UniMVT’s state-of-the-art performance.

2. Related Works

Uplift models for CATE estimation have evolved from meta learning to deep architectures. Early representation-based methods, such as CFRNet (Shalit et al., 2017) and FlexTENet (Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021), focused on minimizing distribution discrepancies, while X-learner (Künzel et al., 2019) addressed treatment imbalance. To mitigate biases in large-scale observational data, approaches like DESCN (Zhong et al., 2022) and EUEN (Ke et al., 2021) employ entire-space modeling to jointly learn propensity and response functions. For continuous treatments, research has progressed from partition-based methods like DRNet (Schwab et al., 2020) to functional continuity models like VCNet (Nie et al., 2021). Furthermore, recent studies have extended these frameworks to handle complex industrial constraints, including temporal dynamics (Zhang et al., 2024), revenue rankability (He et al., 2024a), and robust estimation under covariate shifts (Wang et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2023; Ai et al., 2024). In industrial systems, recent applications integrate intervention attributes, as seen in EFIN (Liu et al., 2023) for coupon distribution and continuous causal forests for dynamic pricing (Wan et al., 2022). Furthermore, methods have evolved beyond binary outcomes to handle complex objectives: addressing long-tail continuous revenue uplift via ZILN distributions and rank-aware losses (He et al., 2024b), and capturing real-time contexts for personalized streaming interventions via frameworks like CDUM (Meng et al., 2024).

3. Preliminaries

3.1. Notations and Definitions

We formally define the observed dataset as 𝒟={(𝐱i,wi,di,yi)}i=1N\mathcal{D}=\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},w_{i},d_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where:

  • •

    𝐱i∈𝒳⊆ℝk\mathbf{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{k} denotes the context feature vector, encompassing user attributes and historical behaviors.

  • •

    wi∈{0,1}w_{i}\in\{0,1\} is the binary treatment indicator, where wi=1w_{i}=1 signifies exposure to the intervention and wi=0w_{i}=0 indicates the control status.

  • •

    ti∈𝒯⊂ℝ+t_{i}\in\mathcal{T}\subset\mathbb{R}^{+} represents the treatment intensity (e.g., coupon face value or discount magnitude). Note that tit_{i} is observable and non-zero if and only if wi=1w_{i}=1; otherwise, we define ti=0t_{i}=0.

  • •

    yi∈{0,1}y_{i}\in\{0,1\} is the binary click label.

3.2. Causal Assumptions

To accurately quantify the impact of interventions on Click-Through Rate (CTR) variations, we frame the problem within the causal inference paradigm. We establish the identifiability of the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) through standard assumptions and introduce a structural constraint to model the intensity-response relationship effectively.

Assumption 3.1 (Consistency, unconfoundedness and overlap).

Following the standard potential outcomes framework (Rubin, 2005), we adopt the following assumptions to ensure the identifiability of the treatment effect:

  • •

    Consistency: The observed outcome yy for a unit receiving treatment tt is identical to the potential outcome Y⁡(t)Y(t); formally, Y=Y⁡(t)Y=Y(t) if T=tT=t.

  • •

    Unconfoundedness: Given the covariate vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the treatment assignment TT is independent of the potential outcomes; formally, {Y⁡(t)}t∈𝒯⟂⟂T|X\{Y(t)\}_{t\in\mathcal{T}}\perp\!\!\!\perp T\mid X.

  • •

    Overlap: Every unit has a non-zero probability of receiving any treatment level within the domain; formally, 0<P⁡(T=t∣X=𝐱)<10<P(T=t\mid X=\mathbf{x})<1 for all t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T} and 𝐱∈𝒳\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X}.

Assumption 3.2 (Latent Linear Monotonicity).

Motivated by empirical statistics from randomized experiments (Figure 1) and the diminishing marginal utility commonly observed in economics, we avoid imposing a strict linear assumption on the absolute probability scale, which is inherently bounded by [0,1][0,1]. Instead, we postulate a structural assumption in the latent space: the treatment intensity tt exerts a monotonic linear shift on the user’s conversion intention within the log-odds (logit) space. Formally, for a user with features 𝐱\mathbf{x}, there exists a user-specific positive scalar η⁡(𝐱)>0\eta(\mathbf{x})>0 such that the post-treatment logit is shifted proportionally by tt:

(1) logit​(pt​(𝐱))−logit​(p0​(𝐱))=η⁡(𝐱)⋅t,where ​η​(𝐱)>0.\text{logit}(p_{t}(\mathbf{x}))-\text{logit}(p_{0}(\mathbf{x}))=\eta(\mathbf{x})\cdot t,\quad\text{where }\eta(\mathbf{x})>0.

3.3. Problem Formulation

Our primary objective is to disentangle the intrinsic user preference (Base CTR) from the intervention effect within the observed data. Building upon this, we aim to accurately estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) across continuous treatment intensities. We frame this problem under the Neyman-Rubin Potential Outcome framework (Rubin, 2005).

Definition 3.0 (Base & Treated CTR).

For a user instance with feature vector 𝐱\mathbf{x}, let Y⁡(t)Y(t) denote the potential outcome when the user is exposed to an intervention intensity t∈𝒯t\in\mathcal{T}, where t=0t=0 specifically denotes the control state (no intervention). We define the Base CTR, denoted as p0​(𝐱)p_{0}(\mathbf{x}), and the Treated CTR, denoted as pt​(𝐱,t)p_{t}(\mathbf{x},t), as the expected potential outcomes conditional strictly on the user covariates:

(2) p0​(𝐱)\displaystyle p_{0}(\mathbf{x}) ≜𝔼⁡[Y⁡(0)∣𝐱],\displaystyle\triangleq\mathbb{E}[Y(0)\mid\mathbf{x}],
(3) pt​(𝐱,t)\displaystyle p_{t}(\mathbf{x},t) ≜𝔼⁡[Y⁡(t)∣𝐱].\displaystyle\triangleq\mathbb{E}[Y(t)\mid\mathbf{x}].
Definition 3.0 (Latent Unit Sensitivity (uCATE)).

Building upon Assumption 3.2, we formally define the scalar parameter η⁡(𝐱)\eta(\mathbf{x}) as the Latent Unit CATE (uCATE). It represents the intrinsic marginal sensitivity of user 𝐱\mathbf{x} to the intervention in the log-odds space. Consequently, the standard Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) in the observable probability space, defined as the absolute difference between potential outcomes, can be systematically parameterized by this intensity-invariant uCATE:

τ⁡(𝐱,t)\displaystyle\tau(\mathbf{x},t) ≜pt​(𝐱,t)−p0​(𝐱)\displaystyle\triangleq p_{t}(\mathbf{x},t)-p_{0}(\mathbf{x})
(4) =σ⁡(logit​(p0​(𝐱))+η⁡(𝐱)⋅t)−p0​(𝐱).\displaystyle=\sigma\Big(\text{logit}(p_{0}(\mathbf{x}))+\eta(\mathbf{x})\cdot t\Big)-p_{0}(\mathbf{x}).

Through this definition, the standard CATE τ⁡(𝐱,t)\tau(\mathbf{x},t) inherently captures the non-linear saturation effect as the intensity tt increases, while maintaining a tractable and optimizable scalar η⁡(𝐱)\eta(\mathbf{x}) for downstream cost-constrained allocation.

4. Framework

4.1. Overview

As illustrated in Figure 2, our framework comprises two modules. The first is a Deconfounded Causal Representation (DCR) Layer, which employs a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) structure to encode input covariates and explicitly disentangle them into treatment-sensitive representations and treatment-invariant confounding representations. The second is a Heterogeneous Treatment Effect (HTE) Network, which leverages these disentangled embeddings to jointly estimate the baseline CTR p0​(𝐱)p_{0}(\mathbf{x}) and the latent unit sensitivity η⁡(𝐱)\eta(\mathbf{x}). Guided by Definition 3.2, the intensity-dependent uplift τ⁡(𝐱,t)\tau(\mathbf{x},t) is subsequently derived analytically for any specific intervention intensity tt. The training strategy uses all observational data, including both coupon and no-coupon populations, to facilitate learning across the full covariate-treatment space.

4.2. Deconfounded Causal Representation

The Deconfounded Causal Representation (DCR) module employs a Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) architecture (Ma et al., 2018c) to encode input features 𝐱i\mathbf{x}_{i} into disentangled latent embeddings. We instantiate three distinct groups of MLP-based experts: Base (𝐇ib\mathbf{H}_{i}^{b}), Shared (𝐇is\mathbf{H}_{i}^{s}), and Treatment (𝐇it\mathbf{H}_{i}^{t}) experts, which capture global baseline preferences, treatment-invariant confounders, and intervention-sensitive features, respectively.

To synthesize these representations, task-specific gating networks (𝐠i0\mathbf{g}_{i}^{0} and 𝐠it\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t}) generate soft attention weights. We construct the final disentangled embeddings, 𝐮i0\mathbf{u}_{i}^{0} and 𝐮it\mathbf{u}_{i}^{t}, using a Stop-Gradient (𝖲𝖦\mathsf{SG}) operator to prevent gradient leakage between conflicting objectives while allowing information flow through shared confounders:

(5) 𝐮i0\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{i}^{0} =(𝐠i0)⊤​𝖢𝖮𝖭𝖢𝖠𝖳​(𝐇ib,𝐇is,𝖲𝖦⁡(𝐇it)),\displaystyle=(\mathbf{g}_{i}^{0})^{\top}\mathsf{CONCAT}\Big(\mathbf{H}_{i}^{b},\mathbf{H}_{i}^{s},\mathsf{SG}(\mathbf{H}_{i}^{t})\Big),
(6) 𝐮it\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{i}^{t} =(𝐠it)⊤​𝖢𝖮𝖭𝖢𝖠𝖳​(𝖲𝖦⁡(𝐇ib),𝐇is,𝐇it).\displaystyle=(\mathbf{g}_{i}^{t})^{\top}\mathsf{CONCAT}\Big(\mathsf{SG}(\mathbf{H}_{i}^{b}),\mathbf{H}_{i}^{s},\mathbf{H}_{i}^{t}\Big).

Consistent with Definition 3.2, 𝐮i0\mathbf{u}_{i}^{0} is fed into the Base Tower to estimate the counterfactual baseline p0​(𝐱i)p_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i}), while 𝐮it\mathbf{u}_{i}^{t} enters the Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Net (HTENet) to directly estimate the Latent Unit CATE η⁡(𝐱i)\eta(\mathbf{x}_{i}).

Furthermore, to explicitly enforce the disentanglement of confounding factors from treatment-specific heterogeneity, we impose an orthogonality penalty (Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021) across all distinctive expert pairs:

(7) ℛo​r​t​h=∑l=1L∑(u,v)∈𝒫‖(𝚯ul)⊤​𝚯vl‖F2,\mathcal{R}_{orth}=\sum_{l=1}^{L}\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}}\left\|(\mathbf{\Theta}^{l}_{u})^{\top}\mathbf{\Theta}^{l}_{v}\right\|_{F}^{2},

where 𝚯(⋅)l\mathbf{\Theta}^{l}_{(\cdot)} denotes the ll-th layer weight matrix of the respective expert group, 𝒫={(b,s),(t,s),(b,t)}\mathcal{P}=\{(b,s),(t,s),(b,t)\}, and ∥⋅∥F2\|\cdot\|_{F}^{2} is the squared Frobenius norm. This constraint minimizes the correlation between the parameter spaces of different expert groups, encouraging the extraction of strictly non-overlapping causal representations.

4.3. Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Net

To prevent task interference and negative transfer between factual and counterfactual estimations, we employ a decoupled tower architecture. We formally define the Heterogeneous Treatment Effect (HTE) Network, consisting of two distinct prediction pathways and a specific mechanism for injecting treatment information.

4.3.1. Decoupled Prediction Towers

To isolate the baseline propensity from intervention-specific dynamics, we instantiate two independent MLP towers:

  • •

    Base Tower: Ingests the baseline-specific representation 𝐮i0\mathbf{u}_{i}^{0} from the DCR layer to estimate the intrinsic click probability p^0​(𝐱i)\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i}).

  • •

    Treatment Tower: Consumes the treatment-aware representation 𝐮it\mathbf{u}_{i}^{t} and the treatment attribute embedding 𝐞it\mathbf{e}^{t}_{i} to predict the intervention-conditioned outcome p^t​(𝐱i,ti)\hat{p}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{i},t_{i}).

To mitigate the signal dilution inherent in simple feature concatenation, we introduce a Treatment-Aware Gate (TA-Gate), adapting the LHUC framework (Chang et al., 2023b) for continuous interventions. For each hidden layer ll, we compute a context-dependent scaling vector 𝐚i(l)∈(0,2)\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(l)}\in(0,2) derived from the treatment embedding 𝐞it\mathbf{e}^{t}_{i}:

(8) 𝐚i(l)=2⋅σ⁡(𝐖g(l)​𝐞it+𝐛g(l)),𝐡~i(l)=𝐚i(l)⊙𝐡i(l).\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(l)}=2\cdot\sigma(\mathbf{W}_{g}^{(l)}\mathbf{e}^{t}_{i}+\mathbf{b}_{g}^{(l)}),\quad\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{(l)}=\mathbf{a}_{i}^{(l)}\odot\mathbf{h}_{i}^{(l)}.

Here, σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function and ⊙\odot denotes the element-wise product. This mechanism ensures that the treatment intensity dynamically modulates the feature processing pathway at multiple abstraction levels.

We formulate the optimization objective using the binary cross-entropy loss function, denoted as ℓBCE​(⋅,⋅)\ell_{\text{BCE}}(\cdot,\cdot). Let 𝒞={i∣ti=0}\mathcal{C}=\{i\mid t_{i}=0\} and 𝒯={i∣ti>0}\mathcal{T}=\{i\mid t_{i}>0\} denote the control and treatment groups, respectively. The factual loss functions for the two towers are defined as:

(9) ℒb​a​s​e\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{base} =∑i∈𝒞ℓBCE​(yi,p^0​(𝐱i)),\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}\ell_{\text{BCE}}(y_{i},\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})),
(10) ℒt​r​e​a​t\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{treat} =∑i∈𝒯ℓBCE​(yi,p^t​(𝐱i,ti)).\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\ell_{\text{BCE}}(y_{i},\hat{p}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{i},t_{i})).

4.3.2. Counterfactual X-Network

Inspired by the X-learner (Künzel et al., 2019), we instantiate an X-Network as a bridging module to enable counterfactual reasoning. It shares the bottom representation 𝐮it\mathbf{u}_{i}^{t} to infer hypothetical outcomes under alternative treatment regimes.

To operationalize this for the control group (𝒞\mathcal{C}), where actual intervention intensity is unobserved, we introduce an auxiliary Intensity Prediction Head to impute a feasible hypothetical dosage t^i\hat{t}_{i}. We strictly enforce domain constraints by projecting the latent representation into a physical range [tmin,tmax][t_{\min},t_{\max}]:

(11) t^i\displaystyle\hat{t}_{i} =σ⁡(𝖬𝖫𝖯⁡(𝖲𝖦⁡(𝐮it)))⋅(tmax−tmin)+tmin,\displaystyle=\sigma(\mathsf{MLP}(\mathsf{SG}(\mathbf{u}^{t}_{i})))\cdot(t_{\max}-t_{\min})+t_{\min},
(12) ℒt\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{t} =∑i∈𝒯(λ1​(ti−t^i)2+λ2​|ti−t^i|),\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}\left(\lambda_{1}(t_{i}-\hat{t}_{i})^{2}+\lambda_{2}|t_{i}-\hat{t}_{i}|\right),

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) ensures the normalized prediction lies strictly within (0,1)(0,1). This head is trained exclusively on the treated group 𝒯\mathcal{T} and applied to infer dosages for the control group.

Simultaneously, we estimate the intensity-invariant Latent Unit CATE (η^i\hat{\eta}_{i}) via the treatment representation. We employ a ReLU activation to structurally enforce non-negativity, satisfying the monotonicity assumption:

(13) η^i=ReLU​(𝖬𝖫𝖯⁡(𝐮it)).\hat{\eta}_{i}=\text{ReLU}(\mathsf{MLP}(\mathbf{u}^{t}_{i})).

Guided by Definition 3.2, we formulate the cross-network estimators by injecting or removing the latent treatment shift (dosage ×\times sensitivity) in the logit space. Let σ−1​(⋅)\sigma^{-1}(\cdot) denote the logit function. The counterfactual estimations are tailored to the respective groups:

(14) For ​i∈𝒯:p^t′​(𝐱i,ti)=σ⁡(σ−1​(p^0​(𝐱i))+ti⋅η^i),\displaystyle\textbf{For }i\in\mathcal{T}:\quad\hat{p}_{t}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{i};t_{i})=\sigma\Big(\sigma^{-1}(\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))+t_{i}\cdot\hat{\eta}_{i}\Big),
(15) For ​i∈𝒞:p^0′​(𝐱i)=σ⁡(σ−1​(p^t​(𝐱i,t^i))−t^i⋅η^i).\displaystyle\textbf{For }i\in\mathcal{C}:\quad\hat{p}_{0}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{i})=\sigma\Big(\sigma^{-1}(\hat{p}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{i},\hat{t}_{i}))-\hat{t}_{i}\cdot\hat{\eta}_{i}\Big).

Equation 14 reconstructs the treated outcome by augmenting the base prediction with the actual treatment shift ti⋅η^it_{i}\cdot\hat{\eta}_{i}. Conversely, Equation 15 reconstructs the baseline for control users by stripping the imputed treatment shift t^i⋅η^i\hat{t}_{i}\cdot\hat{\eta}_{i} from their hypothetical treated prediction.

To enforce consistency between these counterfactual deductions and the factual observed labels, we employ Mean Squared Error (MSE) regularization:

(16) ℒx-treat\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-treat}} =∑i∈𝒯(yi−p^t′​(𝐱i,ti))2,\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}(y_{i}-\hat{p}_{t}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{i};t_{i}))^{2},
(17) ℒx-base\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-base}} =∑i∈𝒞(yi−p^0′​(𝐱i))2.\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}(y_{i}-\hat{p}_{0}^{\prime}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))^{2}.

This mutual regularization propagates supervision from treated to control (and vice versa) via the η^i\hat{\eta}_{i} parameter, mitigating selection bias and implicitly calibrating the latent sensitivity. The combined regularization loss is ℒX=ℒx-treat+ℒx-base\mathcal{L}_{X}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-treat}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-base}}.

The full HTENet is optimized end-to-end via the joint loss:

(18) ℒ=λb​a​s​e​ℒb​a​s​e+λt​r​e​a​t​ℒt​r​e​a​t+λt​ℒt+λX​ℒX+λo​ℛo,\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{base}\mathcal{L}_{base}+\lambda_{treat}\mathcal{L}_{treat}+\lambda_{t}\mathcal{L}_{t}+\lambda_{X}\mathcal{L}_{X}+\lambda_{o}\mathcal{R}_{o},

where λ(⋅)\lambda_{(\cdot)} are hyperparameters balancing factual accuracy, intensity imputation, counterfactual consistency, and orthogonality.

4.4. Theoretical Analysis

To theoretically justify the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we analyze the convergence properties of the unit uplift estimator. We show that under mild assumptions regarding the dosage distribution and the consistency of base estimators, the proposed counterfactual calibration loss guarantees the identification of the true unit uplift.

Assumption 4.1 (Non-trivial Intensity and Common Support).

The treatment intensity tt is bounded away from zero, i.e., there exists a constant tm​i​n>0t_{min}>0 such that |t|≥tm​i​n|t|\geq t_{min} almost surely for all valid interventions. Furthermore, the conditional distribution of feasible intensities P⁡(t|x)P(t|x) depends solely on the feature set xx. The support of the potential intensity distribution in the control group is contained within the support of the treated group:

(19) supp​(P⁡(t∣𝐱,i∈𝒞))⊆supp​(P⁡(t∣𝐱,i∈𝒯)).\text{supp}(P(t\mid\mathbf{x},i\in\mathcal{C}))\subseteq\text{supp}(P(t\mid\mathbf{x},i\in\mathcal{T})).
Assumption 4.2 (Consistency of Base Estimators).

The estimators for the treated outcome y^t\hat{y}_{t} and the intensity t^\hat{t} are consistent, meaning that as the sample size N→∞N\to\infty, p^t→𝑝pt\hat{p}_{t}\xrightarrow{p}p_{t} and t^→𝑝t\hat{t}\xrightarrow{p}t.

Based on these assumptions, we establish the following theorem regarding the convergence of the unit uplift estimator η^\hat{\eta}.

Theorem 4.1 (Convergence of Unit Uplift).

Under Assumptions 4.1 and 4.2, minimizing the counterfactual calibration loss ℒx−t​r​e​a​t\mathcal{L}_{x-treat} and ℒx−b​a​s​e\mathcal{L}_{x-base} ensures that the estimated unit uplift η^\hat{\eta} converges in probability to the true unit uplift η\eta.

Proof Sketch. We take ℒx−t​r​e​a​t\mathcal{L}_{x-treat} as an example; ℒx−b​a​s​e\mathcal{L}_{x-base} can be proven in the same manner. Recall the Assumption3.2 that the counterfactual calibration loss for the control group enforces the constraint: p0​(𝐱i)+η⋅t≈pt​(𝐱i,ti){p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})+{\eta}\cdot{t}\approx{p}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{i},t_{i}).

Let Δ=|η^−η|\Delta=|\hat{\eta}-\eta| be the objective to be minimized. Substituting the true pt​(𝐱i,ti){p}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{i},t_{i}), we analyze the error term:

(20) ℒx-treat\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-treat}} =|(p^0​(𝐱i)+η^​t^)−(p0​(𝐱i)+η⋅t)|\displaystyle=|(\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})+\hat{\eta}\hat{t})-({p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})+{\eta}\cdot{t})|

By the triangle inequality and adding the cross-term η^​t\hat{\eta}{t}, we have:

(21) ℒx-treat\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-treat}} =|(p^0​(𝐱i)−p0​(𝐱i))+(η^​t^−η​t)|\displaystyle=|(\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))+(\hat{\eta}\hat{t}-\eta t)|
(22) =|(p^0​(𝐱i)−p0​(𝐱i))+η^​(t^−t)+t⁡(η^−η)|\displaystyle=|(\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i}))+\hat{\eta}(\hat{t}-t)+{t}(\hat{\eta}-\eta)|

Minimizing ℒx-treat\mathcal{L}_{\text{x-treat}} implies Δ→0\Delta\to 0.

By Assumption 4.2, the terms |p^0​(𝐱i)−p0​(𝐱i)||\hat{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-{p}_{0}(\mathbf{x}_{i})| and |t^−t||\hat{t}-t| converge to 0. Thus, the convergence of the loss relies on the term t⁡(η^−η)→0{t}(\hat{\eta}-\eta)\to 0. By Assumption 4.1, since |t^|→|t|≥tmin>0|\hat{t}|\to|t|\geq t_{\min}>0, the intensity is non-degenerate. Therefore, the only solution for the term to vanish is η^−η→0\hat{\eta}-\eta\to 0. This completes the proof that η^→𝑝η\hat{\eta}\xrightarrow{p}\eta. □\square

4.5. Inference

At inference, UniMVT directly outputs the estimated unit sensitivity η^i\hat{\eta}_{i} and the base conversion probability p^0​(xi)\hat{p}_{0}(x_{i}) for each user ii. To guide coupon allocation decisions, we simulate outcomes over a discrete grid of candidate coupon values q∈{q1,q2,…,qmax}q\in\{q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{\max}\}.

First, we calculate the incremental conversion probability (Uplift) parameterized by qq:

Δ​CTRi​(q)\displaystyle\Delta\text{CTR}_{i}(q) =p^t​(xi,q)−p^0​(xi)\displaystyle=\hat{p}_{t}(x_{i};q)-\hat{p}_{0}(x_{i})
(23) =σ⁡(σ−1​(p^0​(xi))+η^i⋅q)−p^0​(xi)\displaystyle=\sigma(\sigma^{-1}(\hat{p}_{0}(x_{i}))+\hat{\eta}_{i}\cdot q)-\hat{p}_{0}(x_{i})

Then, we formulate a non-linear marginal ROI objective. By incorporating the saturation effect of the sigmoid function and the expected redemption probability γ\gamma, the expected cost inherently acts as a non-linear regularizer against the coupon face value:

(24) ROIi​(q)=Δ​CTRi​(q)𝔼​[Costi​(q)]=p^t​(xi,q)−p^0​(xi)q⋅p^t​(xi,q)⋅γ\displaystyle\text{ROI}_{i}(q)=\frac{\Delta\text{CTR}_{i}(q)}{\mathbb{E}[\text{Cost}_{i}(q)]}=\frac{\hat{p}_{t}(x_{i};q)-\hat{p}_{0}(x_{i})}{q\cdot\hat{p}_{t}(x_{i};q)\cdot\gamma}

The optimal intervention q∗q^{*} is determined by evaluating q∗=arg⁡maxq​ROIi​(q)q^{*}=\arg\max_{q}\text{ROI}_{i}(q). If the optimal ROIi​(q∗)\text{ROI}_{i}(q^{*}) exceeds a system-defined threshold λ\lambda, the voucher q∗q^{*} is issued; otherwise, the treatment is withheld (q=0q=0).

5. Experiment

We evaluate three questions: RQ1, how UniMVT compares with the baselines; RQ2, how each component contributes; and RQ3, how UniMVT performs in online deployment.

5.1. Evaluation Setup

5.1.1. Dataset

We evaluate our approach on both synthetic and real-world datasets to demonstrate its efficacy.

Synthetic Datasets: To evaluate the model against known causal ground truth, we synthesize three controlled benchmarks (Syn-1, Syn-2, and Syn-3) that closely mimic operational marketing environments. Each dataset contains 80,000 training samples and 8,000 test samples, with the test set consisting exclusively of unbiased Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT) samples.

Two design choices ensure industrial relevance. First, the individualized treatment-response curves strictly follow Assumption 3.2. Injecting monotonic linear shifts in logit space preserves probability bounds and produces the nonlinear saturation observed in practice. Second, treatment intensity TT follows unimodal distributions in Syn-1/Syn-2 and a multimodal distribution in Syn-3, reflecting production coupon tiers. We introduce realistic selection bias by confounding TT with user covariates 𝐗\mathbf{X}, so high-value users have a higher propensity to receive high-intensity interventions.

Real-world Dataset: We curate an offline set from Kuaishou live-stream coupon traffic, including both non-intervened organic interactions and interactions subject to heterogeneous intervention intensities. Inputs encompass user profiles, live-stream-room context, and coupon descriptors such as intensity and style, yielding a production-scale CTR task with multi-valued interventions.

5.1.2. Baselines

We compare UniMVT with S-Learner and T-Learner (Künzel et al., 2019), FlexTENet (Curth and Van der Schaar, 2021), CFRNet (Shalit et al., 2017), DRNet (Schwab et al., 2020), VCNet (Nie et al., 2021), and DESCN (Zhong et al., 2022). We extend binary-treatment baselines by using intensity tt as an input; for models predicting full uplift, setting t=1t=1 yields comparable unit uplift, τ^u​n​i​t=Model​(X,t=1)\hat{\tau}_{unit}=\text{Model}(X,t=1).

5.1.3. Evaluation Metrics

We use separate metrics for CTR debiasing and uplift ranking.

Basic CTR Prediction: AUC and LogLoss measure ranking and calibration of the counterfactual conversion probability under control (no treatment).

Multi-valued Uplift Estimation: Binary uplift metrics are insufficient for continuous treatments, so we use a Cumulative Slope (CS) framework. For a test set 𝒪\mathcal{O} of size NN, samples are ranked by predicted Latent Unit CATE η^​(𝐱)\hat{\eta}(\mathbf{x}). Let 𝒪ϕ\mathcal{O}_{\phi} be the top ϕ\phi fraction, ϕ∈[0,1]\phi\in[0,1], and β^​(ϕ)\hat{\beta}(\phi) the regression slope of outcome YY on intensity TT within 𝒪ϕ\mathcal{O}_{\phi}.

Definition 5.0 (CS-AUUC).

The Cumulative Slope Area Under the Uplift Curve (CS-AUUC) measures rank-ordered sensitivity as the area under the realized slope β^​(ϕ)\hat{\beta}(\phi) scaled by bucket size:

(25) CS-AUUC=∫01β^​(ϕ)⋅(ϕ​N)​𝑑ϕ.\displaystyle\text{CS-AUUC}=\int_{0}^{1}\hat{\beta}(\phi)\cdot(\phi N)\,d\phi.

Higher CS-AUUC means more intensity-sensitive users are ranked first.

Definition 5.0 (CS-Qini).

The Cumulative Slope Qini (CS-Qini) measures ranking gain over random targeting. With βglobal\beta_{\text{global}} denoting the average slope on 𝒪\mathcal{O},

(26) CS-Qini=∫01(β^​(ϕ)−βglobal)⋅(ϕ​N)​𝑑ϕ.\displaystyle\text{CS-Qini}=\int_{0}^{1}\left(\hat{\beta}(\phi)-\beta_{\text{global}}\right)\cdot(\phi N)\,d\phi.

Thus CS-Qini quantifies the incremental gain of personalized over random allocation.

5.2. Main Results (RQ1)

Table 1 presents a comprehensive comparison between UniMVT and seven baselines across synthetic and production datasets.

Base CTR Evaluation: The T-Learner’s superiority over the S-Learner indicates that decoupled pathways are crucial for isolating base conversion propensity. Building on this, UniMVT achieves highly competitive, often state-of-the-art AUC and LogLoss. This confirms that our DCR layer successfully disentangles treatment-invariant representations from intervention signals.

Uplift Evaluation: UniMVT establishes a dominant advantage. While baselines like DRNet perform adequately on simple unimodal data, their efficacy degrades significantly in complex multimodal (Syn-3) and industrial (Prod) settings, often yielding near-random CS-Qini scores (Figure 3). This suggests that traditional models are excessively confounded by the absolute treatment magnitude tt, assigning higher scores to larger coupon values rather than capturing intrinsic user sensitivity.

Conversely, UniMVT consistently achieves the highest CS-AUUC and CS-Qini across all scenarios. By explicitly modeling the Latent Unit CATE η⁡(𝐱)\eta(\mathbf{x}) and leveraging X-Network regularization, our framework accurately prioritizes users with genuine treatment sensitivity, demonstrating its robustness and scalability for real-world marketing interventions.

5.3. Ablation Analysis (RQ2)

Table 2 confirms that each component is necessary. Removing DCR degrades all metrics, while omitting X-Network collapses CS-Qini, validating their roles in disentanglement and counterfactual regularization. Removing linear monotonicity through non-logit shifts or unconstrained fitting also drives CS-Qini near zero despite high Base CTR AUC: without structural causal priors, deep networks optimize factual accuracy while overfitting observational bias.

5.4. Online A/B Test (RQ3)

We conducted an online A/B test for UniMVT on a randomly sampled 10% of Kuaishou’s production traffic. Treatment and control buckets were mutually exclusive to prevent interference. We compare our approach against two established production baselines:

  • •

    Base (Two-Stage Model): The legacy production approach independently trains separate learners for base CTR and residual uplift. It suffers from error accumulation and fails to capture shared causal dynamics.

  • •

    Unified Model (Shared-Bottom): A multi-task framework uses a shared encoder with separate prediction towers to jointly estimate base CTR and uplift, representing a stronger representation-learning baseline.

To evaluate online performance, we monitor business metrics—Revenue (Δ\DeltaRev) and Return on Investment (Δ\DeltaROI)—and calibration accuracy via Predicted Click-Over-Click Error (PCOC-Err=|PCOC−1|\text{PCOC-Err}=|\text{PCOC}-1|).

As shown in Table 3, UniMVT consistently outperforms the baselines. Compared with the Base Two-Stage model, it increases coupon revenue by 18.14% and overall ROI by 8.80. Moreover, UniMVT reduces coupon PCOC-Err by 86.51% and no-coupon PCOC-Err by 50.00%. This substantial calibration improvement confirms that DCR and X-Network effectively isolate causal signals from confounding biases, enabling precise and granular coupon allocation.

Following the A/B test, UniMVT has been fully deployed in Kuaishou’s live-stream direct-response ad slots, with ongoing expansion to other marketing scenarios.

6. Conclusion

We proposed UniMVT to address confounding in multi-valued treatments by combining disentangled representation learning with full-space counterfactual inference. Offline and online results, supported by convergence guarantees, demonstrate improved debiased CTR estimation, heterogeneous uplift modeling, and marketing efficiency. Future work will explore more complex treatment-response curves.

We used ChatGPT strictly for language polishing and text refinement of author-written content to improve the manuscript’s readability. No generative AI tools were used for research design, code or data generation, experiments, analysis, results, conclusions, or figure creation.
